title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6489 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: Swiss inflation surprises higher in October but core prices offer some relief
body: Switzerland October CPI +1.5% vs +1.3% y/y expected Prior +1.0% Switzerland October core CPI +0.5% y/y Prior +0.5% Swiss headline annual inflation picks up at the start of the third quarter, rising to 1.5% from 1.0% previously. Much like elsewhere around the region, higher energy prices are the main culprit in continuing to feed through to consumer prices. As such, the inflation numbers may look to be heating up again at first glance. But in looking to core annual inflation, that remains unchanged at just 0.5%. That tells us that the broader inflation picture isn't quite as alarming as the headline reading might suggest. And for the SNB, that is the most crucial takeaway here. The central bank has been arguing for months that higher energy costs are largely responsible for the inflation pickup, with limited evidence of second-round effects spilling over to the wider economy. The latest figures we're seeing today doesn't really challenge that narrative as such. Naturally, headline inflation moving closer to the 2% mark does mean that policymakers won't be entirely comfortable if energy prices continue to stay elevated. That will especially be the case if there is more evidence of businesses eventually passing those higher costs on to consumers. But at least for now, the SNB still has room to sit comfortably on the sidelines and assess how persistent these inflation pressures might become. In other words, there's no reason to panic just yet.

title: US-Iran deal still out of reach despite fresh diplomatic hopes ahead of US midterms
body: And round and round we go. We started the week with renewed optimism that the US and Iran might finally be inching towards a diplomatic breakthrough. That led to oil prices tumbling on Monday as hopes of a potential deal gathered momentum. But fast forward to today, and we're pretty much back where we started. Anyone got a case of déjà vu? These have been the same sort of headlines that we have been dealing with for almost seven months now. The latest comments from a senior Iranian official to Reuters: Tehran's conditions must be met if the US wants the Strait of Hormuz reopened, with nuclear talks only possible afterwards Iran is prepared to respond forcefully to US strikes, both in the region and beyond Mediators are working hard to narrow gaps between Tehran and Washington Now, that is hardly the language of two sides getting ready to shake hands. The thing about all this is that the sticking point remains the same. Iran wants its demands addressed before reopening the Strait of Hormuz, while the US is not willing to agree to those terms. And despite the diplomatic exchanges, neither side appears ready to make the concessions needed to break the deadlock. For markets, it just exemplifies the narrative that the underlying geopolitical risks haven't gone anywhere. While Monday's selloff in the oil market may have shown how quickly traders were willing to price in a potential easing of tensions, the fact of the matter is the reality is not quite there yet.

title: RBA governor Bullock says it might be that this rate hike might not be enough
body: In case you missed it, the RBA raised its cash rate by 25 bps to 4.85% today in a less straightforward 6-3 vote. That takes the cash rate to the highest level in 18 years, with the central bank trying not to pre-commit to further tightening at this stage. So far, Bullock's tone in her press conference has been more neutral and even in the latest remarks here. She says that the rate hike today might not be the last one but in trying to make that judgment, "it is not as obvious" as compared to before. Adding that she doesn't know how high rates will need to go and that it is up to the market to interpret their messaging. Bullock continues to reaffirm that the central bank will stay on a data-dependent path in saying that "it is probably good to wait now and assess incoming data". Having said that, she continues to at least highlight that inflation remains a key concern heading into next year. But at least for now, the dissenting votes should tone down any overly hawkish expectations from the central bank for the immediate outlook. As mentioned here, markets were not pricing in strong odds of another rate hike to follow up the one today. And so, the RBA is reaffirming those expectations for the most part with their choice of language and communique this week.

title: Apple earnings beat fails to impress Wall Street as tech shares struggle ahead of US midterms
body: Another week and it's another big tech name that is finding out that even beating earnings estimates isn't good enough for Wall Street these days. Apple is that next big name to be struck down and the timing couldn't be worse for an already battered tech sector in markets. Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $114.48 billion and earnings per share of $2.10, beating expectations of $113.39 billion and $1.99 respectively. Now, that sounds pretty decent no? Well, if only the market reaction shared that view. Apple shares instead are down 2% in after-hours trading as investors turned their attention to the less flattering details. As always, it is all about the guidance. Of note, Apple expects gross margins to decline to around 45-46% for the December quarter, down from 47.9%, as rising memory costs squeeze profitability. Meanwhile, services revenue growth is also projected at just 8-9% and that comes under expectations of around 10.7%. Besides that, there is also the fact that tariff refunds have flattered the latest quarterly results. So, there is good reason to question how much of the latest earnings strength will carry forward to the next one. In any case, we have seen over the past few weeks how Wall Street is turning more and more unforgiving when it comes to techn earnings especially. It's not enough to deliver good numbers anymore and disappointing outlooks are being punished hard.

title: Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) 25bp rate hike, as widely expected
body: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, its fifth increase of 2026 and the highest level since 2008. The decision was far from unanimous, though: six board members voted to hike and three preferred to hold at 4.60%, a split that tempers the hawkish signal. The board said inflation remains elevated and broadly based, and that staff forecasts have been revised materially higher. Inflation is now expected to stay above 3% over the coming year and not to reach the top of the 2% to 3% target band until late 2027, about three quarters later than previously forecast. Higher fuel and commodity prices linked to the Middle East conflict are part of the story, but the RBA also judged domestic capacity pressures to be a little tighter than thought. It noted that firms are passing on costs and that some measures of inflation expectations have risen. AI-related investment is driving rapid price growth in technology goods. The board also acknowledged that its tightening is biting. The economy is slowing, house prices have fallen significantly and unemployment has risen, with the jobless rate now projected to climb further than expected in August. Weaker housing and consumer spending are expected to be partly offset by stronger business investment, including in data centres. Uncertainty remains high, with the RBA flagging scenarios in which inflation runs higher and growth weaker than forecast.

title: After the Binance hack, the simple security rule regulators keep coming back to, hot vs. cold wallets
body: South Korea's financial regulator wants local crypto exchanges to keep more customer assets in cold wallets, offline storage that hackers cannot reach over the internet. The push follows last week's $6.3 billion theft from Binance, which came entirely from the exchange's internet-connected hot wallets. Following the money: the playbook behind the $6.3bn Binance heist and a suspected $106 million theft The Financial Services Commission held an emergency meeting with major exchanges on 2 November. It reviewed how exchanges control access to their systems and approve withdrawals, and urged them to raise the share of assets held offline. It did not set a new legal ratio. The principle behind the request is simple: a hacker can only steal what is reachable online. Understanding the difference between hot and cold wallets explains why that matters, and why it is not a complete answer. What hot and cold wallets are A crypto wallet does not hold coins the way a purse holds cash. The coins live on the blockchain. What the wallet holds is the private key, a secret code that authorises spending. Whoever controls the key controls the coins. The difference between hot and cold is where that key sits. Hot wallet: the key is on a device or system connected to the internet. That makes it fast and convenient. An exchange can process thousands of withdrawals a day automatically, and an individual can trade or pay from a phone app in seconds.

title: Following the money: the playbook behind the $6.3bn Binance heist and a suspected $106 million theft
body: Two crypto thefts in less than a week show the same playbook. Stolen crypto moves along a predictable path, and the path is shaped by one fear above all others: being frozen. Knowing that path helps explain how much stolen money can be recovered, how much cannot, and why some of it may eventually reach the market. The big one is Binance. On 29 October, an attacker moved about $6.36 billion out of the exchange's hot wallets across ten blockchains, most of it in roughly 20 minutes, according to blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs. A hot wallet is an internet-connected wallet an exchange uses to process withdrawals. The FBI has attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group, and it is the largest crypto theft on record. The smaller case is unconfirmed. Blockchain investigator ZachXBT said on Monday that an unnamed entity in the European Union may have lost more than $106 million from accounts at several exchanges on Sunday. Neither the victim nor the exchanges have been named, so treat it as a suspected theft. It is still useful, because the funds appear to have taken the same route. Step 1: Get out of stablecoins, fast Stablecoins such as Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC are the thief's biggest problem. Their issuers can freeze tokens sitting in a specific wallet, which turns stolen dollars into dead weight. That is exactly what happened at Binance.
